memos.headline: S09 and S02 Lead on Relative Strength; S05 and S10 in Technical Freefall
memos.body: I see a sharply bifurcated universe as of 2025-03-28. S09 stands out as the clear leader: +11.3% over 12 weeks, trading 6.2% above its 50-day mean and only 6.1% off its 52-week high, with RSI at 66 — strong but not yet overbought. S02 has also turned, posting +8.6% over 4 weeks with +15.1% relative strength vs SPY on that timeframe, though the 17.5% drawdown from highs and price still 5.4% below the 200-day mean temper my conviction. On the downside, S05 is the weakest name: RSI 32.8, down 25.2% from its high, 14.2% below its 50-day mean, and showing -13.8% relative strength vs SPY over 12 weeks — this is a falling knife I want no part of. S10 is similarly broken at -26.6% from highs with extreme negative relative strength. I would need to see S05 reclaim 165 and S10 reclaim 120 before reconsidering.

views.note: Strongest trend in the universe: above both moving averages, +12.2% 4w relative strength vs SPY, RSI 66 with room to run; would reassess below 112.
Sharp 4w reversal with +15.1% relative strength vs SPY, but still 5.4% below 200d mean and 17.5% off highs — early-stage recovery; invalidated below 490.
Flat and stable: only 6.5% off highs, hugging both moving averages with RSI 48 — no edge either way, but relative outperformance vs SPY is constructive.
Positive 12w and 26w returns with +7.0% relative strength vs SPY over 12w, but 5.6% below 50d mean suggests a pullback in progress; watching 235 as support.
RSI 32.8, -25.2% drawdown, -14.2% below 50d mean, worst relative strength in the universe at -13.8% over 12w — classic falling knife.
Down 26.6% from highs with 4.56% ATR and -14.7% 12w relative strength vs SPY; extreme weakness with no sign of stabilization.
RSI 37.3, 11.1% below 50d mean, and -20.4% drawdown despite positive 26w return — intermediate trend has broken down decisively.
Down 20.9% from highs, 8.7% below 200d mean, RSI 38 — persistent downtrend, though 4w relative strength vs SPY is slightly positive.
RSI 37.6, 10.3% below 200d mean, -19% drawdown; 4w relative strength vs SPY is mildly positive but not enough to offset the structural damage.
Mid-range weakness: 5.4% below 50d mean, RSI 41.5, -15.9% drawdown — not as broken as S05/S10 but no reason to step in front of this yet.

memos.headline: S10's 56% Net Margin and 78% Revenue Growth Stand Out; S09 and S02 Show Earnings Stagnation
memos.body: I see the clearest durable earnings power in S10, which posted $39.3B in revenue (+77.9% YoY) with a remarkable 56.2% net margin and only $8.5B in total debt — a pristine balance sheet for that scale. S05 and S04 also impress with double-digit revenue growth (11.8% and 12.3% respectively) and net margins north of 27%, though S04 carries $45B in debt that I want to watch. On the other end, S02 delivered only 5.5% net margin on $100.8B revenue with $76.9B in debt and net income growth of just 1.6% YoY — that is thin earnings power relative to leverage. S09 is similarly unattractive: revenue declined 1.1% YoY, net income was essentially flat, and the 9.1% margin leaves little cushion. I would change my view on S09 and S02 if I saw margin expansion above 12% or meaningful debt reduction in the next filing.

views.note: 77.9% revenue growth, 56.2% net margin, and minimal debt of $8.5B make this the strongest fundamental profile in the universe.
Revenue up 11.8% to $96.5B with 27.5% net margin and low debt of $14.8B signals durable, high-quality earnings.
12.3% revenue growth and 34.6% net margin are excellent, though $45B in total debt warrants monitoring.
Revenue grew 10.5% and net income nearly doubled, but 10.7% net margin on $187.8B revenue with $58B debt suggests the earnings surge may not be fully durable.
32.7% net margin and 50.5% NI growth are strong, but $401B in total debt (financial institution leverage) makes earnings quality harder to assess from this data alone.
29.2% net margin is solid but revenue growth of only 4% and $94.8B in debt suggest mature, slower compounding.
21.2% net margin and 33.5% NI growth are encouraging, but only 2.1% revenue growth and $25.3B debt on $21.9B revenue limit conviction.
Revenue declined 5% YoY to $16.2B and debt of $31.7B is nearly 2x revenue — earnings power is under pressure.
Revenue down 1.1%, net income flat, 9.1% margin, and $36.8B in debt — no evidence of improving earnings trajectory.
Only 5.5% net margin and 1.6% NI growth on $76.9B debt is the weakest margin-to-leverage profile in the universe.

memos.headline: Fed on Pause at 4.50% With Sticky Inflation—Favor Defensives and Banks Over Duration-Sensitive Growth
memos.body: I see the Fed firmly in pause mode: the upper bound has been unchanged at 4.50% for three months, even as the trailing 12-month rate cut totals 100 bp. CPI is running at +2.8% y/y, still above target, while unemployment sits at 4.2%—flat over three months but up 30 bp y/y, signaling a mild labor market softening rather than outright weakness. The 10y yield has dropped 35 bp over three months to 4.27%, and the 10y-2y spread has steepened to +0.41 pp (+75 bp y/y), which is consistent with markets pricing eventual easing but no urgency. In this pause-with-sticky-inflation regime, I favor banks (benefiting from a positively sloped curve and stable short rates) and staples (defensive in a slowing economy), while I would avoid pure duration-sensitive growth names that need rate cuts to re-rate. A March CPI print above 0.4% m/m or unemployment jumping above 4.4% would force me to revisit this call.

views.note: Banks benefit from a steepening curve (+41 bp 10y-2y spread) and stable fed funds, supporting net interest margins.
Staples offer defensive positioning as unemployment drifts higher (4.2%) and growth slows without a hard landing.
Cyclicals face mixed signals—labor market softening but no recession; I lack conviction either way.
Duration-sensitive growth is vulnerable while the Fed pauses at 4.50% and CPI remains sticky at 2.8% y/y.
Energy is more commodity-driven than macro-driven; the mild slowdown is a slight headwind but not decisive.
With the 10y at 4.27% and curve steepening, long-duration bond proxies are range-bound until the next CPI surprise.

memos.headline: Post-Earnings Negative Sentiment Dominated Q1; S10 and S05 Saw Sharpest Sell-Offs
memos.body: I see a cluster of negative earnings-driven price reactions across the universe this quarter, with S10 dropping -8.5% on its Feb 26 results, S05 falling -7.3% on Feb 4, S03 declining -4.1% on Feb 6, and S09 slipping -2.5% on Jan 31. These are meaningful one-day moves that signal disappointed expectations, and the question now is whether the negative tone has been fully priced or whether it persists. S05's subsequent Reg FD filing on March 18 suggests management is actively managing the narrative, which could mark a tone inflection. S10's leadership change on March 7 following its earnings miss adds uncertainty rather than resolution. I have more conviction on avoiding names where negative sentiment is fresh and compounded by governance noise (S10), and I'm cautiously watching for a potential tone turn in S05 where management appears to be re-engaging investors.

views.note: Worst earnings reaction at -8.5% compounded by a director/officer change two weeks later signals unresolved negative sentiment.
Sharp -7.3% earnings sell-off in Feb but March Reg FD filing hints at management re-engaging the narrative, possible tone inflection.
The -4.1% earnings reaction was moderate and now seven weeks old; negative tone likely priced but no positive catalyst visible.
Mild -2.5% earnings reaction in late January is stale enough to be largely absorbed; no subsequent filings to shift tone.
Bylaws/rights modification filing is governance noise without an earnings signal; insufficient data to take a directional view.
Shareholder vote filing is routine with no earnings or operational content to drive sentiment.

memos.headline: Policy Uncertainty Tripled in Three Months—Structural Risk Repricing Underway
memos.body: I am focused on the extraordinary surge in the Economic Policy Uncertainty Index, which at 313.11 has risen +200.2% over three months, signaling that the current policy environment—likely driven by tariff escalation, export controls, and broader China-related trade actions—is far beyond a one-quarter event. HY spreads have widened 43bp over the same period to 3.27%, confirming that credit markets are beginning to price geopolitical tail risk even as VIX has pulled back 11.5% over the past month. WTI crude at $70.30 is essentially flat, suggesting energy supply disruptions are not the primary driver and that the uncertainty is concentrated in trade/industrial policy channels. I have moderate conviction that names with high supply-chain concentration in China or significant export-control exposure (S05, S06) face structural headwinds, while domestically oriented or defense-adjacent names may be relatively insulated. A reversal in my view would require a concrete de-escalation in tariff or export-control policy, not merely rhetoric.

views.note: Two 8-Ks in six weeks including Reg FD disclosure amid a tripling of policy uncertainty suggest elevated geopolitical or regulatory exposure.
Early-February 8-K coinciding with the onset of the policy uncertainty spike raises concern about trade-policy or sanctions-related exposure.
Reg FD disclosure in late January predates the worst of the uncertainty surge; insufficient evidence to take a directional view but monitoring closely.
No company-specific filings in evidence; the macro backdrop of widening HY spreads and elevated policy uncertainty warrants caution but not a directional call.
With WTI stable near $70 and no adverse filings, domestically oriented energy or commodity names may benefit from relative insulation against trade-policy shocks.
No specific evidence of geopolitical exposure; the 200% surge in policy uncertainty keeps me cautious across the board absent clarity on tariff scope.

plan.summary: In a highly uncertain macro environment (policy uncertainty tripled, sticky inflation, Fed on pause), I concentrate on the strongest technical trend (S09) while pairing with defensive/macro-favored names (S04, S02) and keeping a large cash buffer. I avoid the technically broken names (S05, S10, S03, S07) despite some having strong fundamentals, as price action and sentiment are hostile near-term.

plans.rationale: Strongest technical profile in the universe: +11.3% over 12 weeks, RSI 66 with room to run, 6.2% above 50-day mean, and positive relative strength vs SPY. Technical analyst has high conviction (0.85 long). Fundamentals are weak (declining revenue, thin margins) which caps sizing, but momentum is clearly the dominant factor near-term.
plans.changes_my_mind: Close below 112 (roughly 5% stop) would break the uptrend structure; also if WTI crude drops below $65 suggesting demand destruction that could weigh on energy-adjacent names.

plans.rationale: Sharp 4-week reversal with +15.1% relative strength vs SPY and macro tailwind from steepening yield curve (+41bp 10y-2y spread) benefiting bank NIM. Technical analyst (0.60 long) and macro analyst (0.65 long) agree on direction. Weak fundamentals (5.5% margin, high debt) and still 17.5% off highs limit conviction and sizing.
plans.changes_my_mind: Close below 490 invalidates the technical recovery thesis; a flattening of the yield curve (10y-2y spread compressing below +20bp) would remove the macro tailwind.

plans.rationale: Defensive staples positioning favored by macro analyst (0.60 long) as unemployment drifts higher without hard landing. Strong fundamentals: 12.3% revenue growth, 34.6% net margin (fundamental analyst 0.75 long). Technical picture is weak (RSI 37.6, -19% drawdown) which is the main risk, but the 3% weekly selloff may offer a better entry for a mean-reversion bounce.
plans.changes_my_mind: Close below 355 (roughly 7% stop) would signal further structural breakdown; March CPI above 0.4% m/m could hurt consumer staples via margin compression.

plans.rationale: Flat and stable with only 6.5% drawdown from highs, hugging moving averages. Technical analyst rates neutral (0.55) with constructive relative strength vs SPY. Decent fundamentals (21.2% margin, 33.5% NI growth). Small position as a low-volatility anchor; macro analyst's concern about duration sensitivity in a paused-Fed environment limits sizing.
